section.title: The Third Journey: Ephesus
section.sectionRationale: The third journey centres on Ephesus, a great city devoted to the goddess Artemis and steeped in magic. Apollos is instructed more accurately, disciples who knew only John's baptism receive the Spirit, and for two years the word spreads from the hall of Tyrannus until all Asia has heard. The gospel exposes counterfeit power in the failure of the sons of Sceva, purges the magic arts, and finally collides with the pagan economy in the silversmiths' riot.
section.thesis: The name of the Lord Jesus, proclaimed and honoured through the Spirit's power, overthrows every rival, the half-knowledge of John's disciples, the counterfeit exorcism of Sceva's sons, the occult books of Ephesus, and the idol trade of Artemis, so that the word of the Lord prevails even against a city's religion and wealth.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the eloquent Apollos taught the way more accurately; the Ephesian disciples who receive the Spirit; two years of preaching from the hall of Tyrannus; the seven sons of Sceva and the burning of the magic books; and the riot of the silversmiths for the sake of Artemis.

units.label: Apollos taught more accurately
units.note: an eloquent man, fervent in spirit

verses.text: After Paul had spent some time in Antioch, he traveled from place to place throughout the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and was fervent in spirit. He spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When Apollos resolved to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On his arrival, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed.
For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

units.label: The Holy Spirit received at Ephesus
units.note: disciples who knew only John's baptism

verses.text: While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the interior and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples
and asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” “No,” they answered, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
“Into what, then, were you baptized?” Paul asked. “The baptism of John,” they replied.
Paul explained: “John’s baptism was a baptism of {{metanoia|repentance}}. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”
On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were about twelve men in all.

units.label: The hall of Tyrannus
units.note: all Asia hears the word of the Lord

verses.text: Then Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God.

But when some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the {{hodos|Way}}, Paul took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.
God did extraordinary {{dynameis|miracles}} through the hands of Paul,
so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, and the diseases and evil spirits left them.

units.label: The seven sons of Sceva
units.note: counterfeit power exposed, the name honoured, the magic burned

verses.text: Now there were some itinerant Jewish exorcists who tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those with evil spirits. They would say, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.”
Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
But one day the evil spirit responded, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?”
Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them all. The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus, and fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds.
And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. When the value of the books was calculated, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas.
So the {{logos|word}} of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail.

units.label: The riot of the silversmiths
units.note: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians

verses.text: After these things had happened, Paul resolved in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. “After I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.”
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he stayed for a time in the province of Asia.
About that time there arose a great disturbance about the Way.
It began with a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, bringing much business to the craftsmen.
Demetrius assembled the craftsmen, along with the workmen in related trades. “Men,” he said, “you know that this business is our source of prosperity.

And you can see and hear that not only in Ephesus, but in nearly the whole province of Asia, this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away. He says that man-made gods are no gods at all.

There is danger not only that our business will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed, she who is worshiped by all the province of Asia and the whole world.”
When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Soon the whole city was in disarray. They rushed together into the theatre, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia.
Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him.
Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre.
Meanwhile the assembly was in turmoil. Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there.
The Jews in the crowd pushed Alexander forward to explain himself, and he motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people.
But when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”

Finally the city clerk quieted the crowd and declared, “Men of Ephesus, doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?
Since these things are undeniable, you ought to be calm and not do anything rash.
For you have brought these men here, though they have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess.
So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there.
But if you are seeking anything beyond this, it must be settled in a legal assembly.
For we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events, and we have no justification to account for this commotion.”
After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.

metanoia.gloss: Repentance, a turning of the mind and life. John's baptism was a baptism of metanoia that pointed forward to the Coming One. It was genuine but preparatory; it needed completion in faith in Jesus and the gift of the Spirit, which is why the Ephesian disciples are baptized into His name.

hodos.gloss: A road or way. In Acts the Way becomes an early name for the Christian faith, the whole life of following Jesus who is Himself the way. At Ephesus the Way is both maligned by opponents and threatened by a riot, yet the word of the Lord prevails against every obstacle in its path.

dynameis.gloss: Mighty works, acts of power, the plural of dynamis. God worked extraordinary dynameis through Paul's hands, but the power is God's, not Paul's or a relic's. The contrast with the sons of Sceva shows that such power belongs only to the name of the Lord Jesus and cannot be borrowed by the faithless.

logos.gloss: Word, message. Luke repeatedly makes the logos of the Lord the true hero of Acts: it spreads, grows, and prevails. At Ephesus, against magic and idolatry alike, the word of the Lord powerfully spreads and triumphs, showing that the gospel advances by God's message, not by spectacle.

basic.context: The third journey settles at Ephesus. First Apollos, mighty in Scripture but knowing only John's baptism, is taught more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila. Then Paul meets disciples who have not received the Spirit; he explains the gospel, baptizes them into Jesus, and the Spirit comes. For two years Paul preaches in the hall of Tyrannus until all Asia hears. The name of Jesus is honoured when the sons of Sceva fail, magic books are burned, and finally the silversmiths riot to defend Artemis.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the chapter as a series of contests between the name of the Lord Jesus and every rival power: partial knowledge, counterfeit exorcism, occult magic, and idol worship tied to money. The key question the Ephesian disciples raise is how and when the Spirit is received. The refrain to watch is that the word of the Lord grows and prevails.
basic.originalLanguages: John's baptism was one of metanoia, repentance, pointing to Christ. Opponents malign the hodos, the Way, yet God works dynameis, mighty acts, through Paul that no one can counterfeit. Above all, the logos, the word, of the Lord spreads and prevails, the true triumph of the chapter over magic and idolatry.
basic.typology: The burning of the magic books pictures the decisive break with the old life that faith in Christ demands. The powerlessness of the sons of Sceva against the demon shows that the name of Jesus is no magic formula but belongs to those who truly know Him. Artemis, the great goddess who seems to rule the city, is exposed as a man-made god who is no god at all.
basic.christ: The name of the Lord Jesus is the theme. It is honoured when counterfeit users fail, confessed when believers turn from magic, and defended by God against the idol trade. His name carries the Spirit's power and cannot be borrowed by the faithless.
basic.god: God pours out the Spirit, works mighty deeds, purges the church of magic, and overrules a riot through a pagan town clerk. He is sovereign over false religion and false power, and His word cannot be stopped by a city's wealth or worship.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians, written to this church, warns against the powers and calls believers to stand in Christ's armor. 1 Corinthians was written from Ephesus. The Spirit coming with tongues echoes Pentecost in Acts 2. The burning of magic books recalls the call to turn wholly from idols.
basic.oneStory: The gospel confronts the pagan world at its centre of religion and magic. The one story of Scripture, God claiming the nations for His Son, advances as the name of Jesus overthrows every rival at Ephesus and the word of the Lord prevails, pressing on toward Rome and the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
Luke builds this chapter as a series of contests, each one a little larger than the last. It begins with a gifted teacher who has part of the truth (Apollos, 18:24-28), moves to twelve men who have even less (19:1-7), then to rival religious opinion in the synagogue (19:8-9), rival power in the hands of the sons of Sceva (19:13-17), rival wealth and ritual in the burned scrolls (19:18-19), and finally a rival goddess defended by a whole city (19:23-41). Two summary statements hold the frame together. Verse 10 says that everyone in Asia heard the word of the Lord, and verse 20 says that the word of the Lord grew and prevailed. Luke uses the same verb for growth in his earlier summaries, Acts 6:7 and 12:24, so the reader hears a refrain that has been sounding since Jerusalem.

The riot is the longest single scene in the chapter and is written with a dramatist's eye. The crowd chants the same slogan twice, the first time out of rage (19:28) and the second out of panic (19:34), and Luke dryly observes that most of them did not know why they had come (19:32). The word he uses for this mob is ekklesia, the ordinary Greek word for an assembly, and he uses it three times for the rioters (19:32, 39, 41). Elsewhere it means the church. The effect is quiet satire: a disorderly crowd borrows the name of the gathering that God is actually building.

There is also a hinge in verse 21. Paul resolves in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome, and from here the book leans toward those two cities. The Ephesian chapter is therefore both the high point of Paul's free ministry and the last scene before the road of chains.
context.historical:
Ephesus sat on the western coast of what is now Turkey, the chief city of the Roman province of Asia and one of the great harbours of the eastern Mediterranean. Its temple of Artemis was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world, and the city called itself the guardian of that temple, which is exactly the title the city clerk uses in 19:35. The goddess of Ephesus was not simply the Greek huntress. She was an older, local mother figure whose image was believed to have fallen from heaven, and the temple also worked as a bank and as an engine of tourism, with pilgrims buying silver shrines as souvenirs and offerings. Demetrius's complaint in 19:25-27 is therefore honest economics wrapped in piety.

Magic was part of daily life. Ephesus had a reputation for charms and spell formulas, and the scrolls in 19:19 were probably handbooks of such formulas. Luke records their value as fifty thousand drachmas. A drachma is often reckoned as roughly a day's wage for a labourer, so the figure is very large, and the people who burned the scrolls did so knowing exactly what it cost. Burning was the one way to make sure no one else would pick them up and use them.

The time is the mid fifties of the first century. Paul first taught in the synagogue for three months, then moved to the lecture hall of Tyrannus for two years (19:8-10), and later told the elders that his stay in Ephesus covered three years (20:31). 1 Corinthians was written from here (1 Corinthians 16:8-9), and Paul speaks elsewhere of terrible pressure in Asia that made him despair of life (2 Corinthians 1:8-10). Luke's cheerful chapter leaves out much of the cost. The theatre of Ephesus was a vast open-air venue, which is why a crowd of that size could gather so quickly. The city clerk and the provincial officials who befriend Paul (19:31) show that Roman administration in Asia was more a shield for the church than an enemy at this stage.
context.canonical:
Ephesus becomes one of the most fully documented churches in the New Testament. Paul writes to it, or to the circle of churches around it, in the letter we call Ephesians. Timothy is later left there to deal with false teachers (1 Timothy 1:3), and the risen Christ addresses the church in Revelation 2:1-7, praising its endurance and testing of false apostles but charging it with having abandoned its first love. The story that began with a handful of half-informed disciples ends with a congregation whose lampstand Christ Himself threatens to remove, a reminder that a church's beginnings do not guarantee its end.

The chapter also gathers up themes from earlier in the Bible. The Law forbade divination, sorcery, spells and the consulting of mediums (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), so the convert who burns his scrolls is obeying a command as old as Sinai. The prophets mocked the idol trade with a sharpness that Demetrius could almost be answering, for Isaiah 44:9-20 pictures the same craftsmen at their forge and bench, and Psalm 115:4-8 says that those who make idols become like them. Paul's line that man-made gods are no gods at all (19:26) is an Old Testament sentence spoken in a Greek city.

The handing on of the Spirit in 19:6 also completes a pattern in Acts. At Pentecost the Spirit comes on Jewish believers (2:1-4), then on the Samaritans (8:14-17), then on the household of Cornelius (10:44-48), and here on a group that stood in the line of John the Baptist. Each time the apostles are present, and each time the same gift is shown to belong to the same Lord. The movement Jesus announced in Acts 1:8 is reaching one more border.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Luke wants his readers, many of them Gentile believers in cities like this one, to see that the gospel does not merely survive among rival powers; it wins an open contest with them. He shows four kinds of rival in turn. There is half-truth in Apollos and the twelve, who are corrected gently and without scandal. There is counterfeit spiritual power in the sons of Sceva, who try to use Jesus's name as a tool and are humiliated by the very spirit they meant to command. There is the old life with its scrolls and its secret practices, which believers confess and burn. And there is the settled religion of a city with a famous temple and a profitable trade.\n\nThe lesson he draws is not triumphalist. The believers do not storm the temple. Paul is held back from the theatre by his own friends, and it is a pagan clerk who calms the crowd. What changes the city is the word spreading through ordinary conversation and the testimony of changed lives. Luke also wants readers to notice how Paul treats Apollos's gaps and the twelve's gaps differently from the sons of Sceva's fraud: ignorance is taught, pretence is exposed. A reader is meant to come away asking whether his own knowledge of Jesus is accurate, and whether anything in his life still belongs to the old trade.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Luke tells us what happened here and almost never tells us what to copy. Nowhere does he command believers to expect tongues at the laying on of hands, to send out handkerchiefs for the sick, or to burn their libraries. The healing cloths in verse 12 are described, not recommended, and Luke is careful to say that it was God who did the miracles through Paul's hands, not the cloth. Compare Acts 5:15, where people hoped Peter's shadow would fall on the sick; Luke records the hope without making a method of it.\n\nWhat does carry forward is the shape of the repentance. Verses 18 and 19 show believers confessing and disclosing their deeds, and then removing what tied them to the old practices at real financial cost, publicly and without bargaining. The principle for today is that a believer deals with whatever still binds him to false power, whether that is an occult object, a habit, or a source of income, and does not argue about the price. The failure of the sons of Sceva also teaches something lasting: the name of Jesus is not a formula that works for anyone who recites it. It belongs to those who actually belong to Him.

debates.question: What do the Ephesian disciples and their rebaptism teach about receiving the Holy Spirit?

views.label: They were not yet Christians; the Spirit comes with true faith in Jesus
views.case: They knew only John's baptism and had not even heard of the Spirit, so they stood on the far side of the gospel, like disciples of John awaiting the Coming One. Paul completes their understanding, they believe in Jesus and are baptized into His name, and only then does the Spirit come. This reads the episode as a unique transitional case, not a second blessing, and it fits the New Testament pattern that all who believe in Christ receive the Spirit, Romans 8:9.

views.label: A subsequent reception of the Spirit after believing
views.case: Others take them as believers who received the Spirit in a distinct, later moment through the laying on of hands, and see here a pattern for a Spirit-reception beyond conversion. They point to Paul's question in verse 2, which can be translated 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?', as if reception and belief could be separated. Rightly weighed, their ignorance of the Spirit and their rebaptism into Jesus mark them as not yet fully Christian, so the passage bridges John's era to the church rather than teaching a normal two-stage experience.

debates.bearing: The episode guards the truth that to belong to Christ is to have His Spirit; it addresses people caught between John's preparatory baptism and full faith in Jesus, and should not be pressed into a routine of Spirit-baptism separated from conversion.

debates.question: Why were these men baptized again when John's baptism was already a baptism of repentance?

views.label: John's baptism was provisional and ended with the coming of Christ
views.case: John himself said that he baptized with water but the One coming after him would baptize with the Holy Spirit, Matthew 3:11. Once the Coming One had come, died and risen, to stay with John's baptism was to remain on the old side of the line. Baptism into the name of the Lord Jesus (19:5) marks entry into what He has done, and so Paul does not treat their earlier baptism as invalid in its day but as insufficient now.

views.label: This is not a rebaptism but the first Christian baptism these men had received
views.case: Others stress that the text says they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus, never that they were rebaptized, and that Apollos in 18:25 was not baptized again even though he too knew only John's baptism. On this reading the Ephesian twelve differed from Apollos in that they lacked even the basic message about Jesus and the Spirit, so their case does not show that every earlier baptism must be repeated.

debates.bearing: Whichever way one reads the grammar, the weight falls on the content of faith, not on the water: a baptism means what the person understands and believes about Jesus, and where that is missing the person must be taught first.

study.originalLanguages:
The most useful place to begin is the exchange in verses 2 and 3. Paul asks whether they received the Holy Spirit pisteusantes, a Greek aorist participle formed from the verb to believe. The BSB renders it 'when you became believers', and the old rendering 'since you believed' is also possible. Greek participles express timing loosely, so Paul's question does not itself settle whether belief and the gift of the Spirit could be separated. The answer comes from context: these men had not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit, which means that whatever they had believed was not yet faith in the Jesus Paul preached.

In verses 18 and 19 the phrase translated 'magic arts' is ta perierga, a plural neuter adjective used as a noun and meaning, roughly, things overdone, curious or meddlesome. In 1 Timothy 5:13 the related word describes busybodies. Luke chooses a word that captures the overreaching curiosity of magic, which tries to reach what God has not given. The same believers 'confessing and disclosing their deeds' use a pair of verbs that suggest open, public declaration, not private regret.

The scene with the evil spirit turns on two different verbs for knowing in verse 15. The spirit says it ginosko Jesus and epistamai Paul. The first suggests recognition of a person it has met and cannot resist; the second suggests acquaintance with a man's reputation. Neither verb is used of the exorcists, to whom it says simply, 'who are you?' The sons of Sceva used the verb horkizo in verse 13, to adjure by an oath, which is the language of formula. They treated the name of Jesus as a borrowed password. The spirit's reply shows that no such thing exists. When the man 'overpowered' them in verse 16, Luke uses katakyrieuo, a compound meaning to gain mastery over. Peter uses the same verb for elders who must not lord it over their flocks, 1 Peter 5:3, a reminder that mastery of this kind belongs to the wrong people.

Verse 12 adds two borrowed Latin words. The 'handkerchiefs' are soudaria and the 'aprons' are simikinthia, both everyday items of a workman's kit, and Luke is deliberately plain about them. Finally, the summary in verse 20 says the word 'grew' (auxano, the same verb as in 6:7 and 12:24) and 'prevailed' (ischuo, to be strong). The pairing makes growth and strength one event: the word spreads because it has the power to win. The chapter ends with ekklesia used three times of the mob, a Greek word that Luke has been keeping for the church.

typology.type: The Spirit on the Ephesian disciples, Acts 19:6
typology.fulfillment: Acts has already shown the Spirit coming on Jews (2:1-4), Samaritans (8:14-17) and Gentiles (10:44-48). Here the same gift reaches men from the line of John the Baptist, so that no group stands outside the work of the one Spirit. It also fulfils John's own promise that the One after him would baptize with the Holy Spirit, Matthew 3:11. The correspondence is Pentecost in miniature, with tongues and prophecy as its sign. The type falls short in one respect only: Pentecost was the founding event, while Ephesus shows the same gift being extended, so the repetition proves the gospel is one, not that every believer must pass through a second scene.

typology.type: The burning of the magic scrolls, Acts 19:19
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told to burn the idols of the nations (Deuteronomy 7:25) and to have nothing to do with sorcery (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). The Ephesian bonfire does what the law commanded in a new setting, and it does so at a cost of fifty thousand drachmas. Christ completes the pattern by taking away the power behind the old arts: He bound the strong man and plundered his house, Mark 3:27, and Colossians 2:15 speaks of rulers and authorities disarmed at the cross. The type is limited in that burning scrolls only removes the tools; it is the Spirit who removes the hold. Believers can burn every book and still carry the old fear unless they are given a new Master.

typology.type: Paul's cloths and Peter's shadow, Acts 19:12 and 5:15
typology.fulfillment: The woman who touched the fringe of Jesus's cloak and was healed, Luke 8:43-48, shows where the power really lives, for Jesus says that power went out from Him. Acts 5:15 and 19:12 carry the same pattern into the apostles' ministry: God honours His messengers by working through what they touch. The escalation is that Christ is the source and the apostles only channels, so Luke is careful to write that God did extraordinary miracles through Paul's hands. The type falls short if turned into a method, because Scripture never says the cloths themselves held any power, and the sons of Sceva show what happens when someone tries to use Jesus's name without belonging to Him.

typology.type: Artemis and the idol craftsmen, Acts 19:24-27
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 44:9-20 pictures the carpenter who burns half the tree to warm himself and makes the rest into a god, and Psalm 115:4-8 says that idols have mouths but cannot speak. Demetrius and his guild are those craftsmen in the flesh, and their shrine business is the idolatry of Isaiah turned into a trade. The fulfilment is that the living God now speaks, in His Son, to the very city that carved its gods. Paul's argument that handmade gods are no gods is the prophetic argument at last pressing on its target. The type falls short in that the satire is not the cure. Mockery exposes the idol, but only the word that Luke says 'grew and prevailed' replaces what the idol could not give.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by showing what He does with His own name. Luke's repeated phrase is the name of the Lord Jesus: in baptism (19:5), in the failed exorcism (19:13-17), and in the honour it receives afterwards (19:17). The point is that the name carries Him. When the exorcists say 'Jesus, whom Paul proclaims', they are borrowing a second hand reputation, and the spirit sees through it. Where Jesus is actually known, His name is not a formula but a person's authority. Philippians 2:9-11 says God gave Him the name above all names, and Acts 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved. Ephesus is a test case of both texts.

The chapter also leads to Christ by contrast. John the Baptist had said that One more powerful would come to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, Matthew 3:11. Apollos and the twelve are the people still living in the preparation. Paul's explanation in 19:4 is that John's baptism told people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus. The Spirit's coming in 19:6 is the proof that the promised Baptizer has acted. Christ does not leave John's disciples at the river.

Christ is also seen as the One who defeats the powers. Ephesians, written to this city's church, says that God raised Christ and seated Him above every rule, authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, Ephesians 1:19-21. The people who read that letter would remember the scrolls, the spirit that overpowered seven men, and the cry of Artemis. Their Lord is above all of it.

We should be careful not to force allegories here, such as treating Artemis's temple as a figure of the church or the number of scroll values as a code. The honest link is that the name which Ephesus tried to use, borrow or drown out is the name of the One who is Lord over everything it feared, and the church there is the first fruit of His claim on that city.
study.god:
This chapter shows God working at three levels at once. He acts in power, giving the Spirit to the twelve and doing extraordinary miracles through Paul. He acts in discipline and mercy, exposing the sons of Sceva while giving believers the courage to confess what they had hidden. And He acts in providence, using a pagan town clerk to disperse a mob that Paul's own friends could not reason with. In Luke's account God is never absent from the riot, though no one in it prays and no sign appears. He works through the clerk's concern for the city's legal standing.

The chapter holds together some tensions that careful readers feel. God is sovereign over the powers of Ephesus, yet He lets them rage, and Paul later calls his time there a fight with wild beasts (1 Corinthians 15:32). God honours His servants, yet He will not allow His name to be used as a charm. God gives the Spirit freely to believers, yet He does so in a sequence that shows His care for each group, Jew, Samaritan, Gentile and disciple of John. The same God who heals through a workman's apron is also the God whose name cannot be commanded.

The chapter also shows the character of the God who is worshipped. Artemis is defended by volume: two hours of shouting, because she cannot answer for herself (19:34). The Lord needs no such defender. His word grows by being spoken, and He is able to turn the opposition's own institutions, the courts and the clerk's legal assembly, to protect His people. The doctrine of God that emerges is that He is the living God, in the language of Paul's earlier sermon, who made heaven and earth and calls people to turn from worthless things to Him, Acts 14:15.

For worship, the chapter teaches that devotion is exclusive and costly. The believers who burned their scrolls were not merely abandoning a hobby; they were declaring who is Lord. Their action invites every worshipper to ask what in his life still belongs to another claim, and to give it up as publicly as they did.

crossReferences.note: Written to this very church, the letter says the struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces. After Acts 19, with its spirit that mastered seven men and its occult scrolls, those words would not sound abstract to the readers. They had seen what the powers were like and where the victory lay.

Paul's clearest statement that having the Spirit and belonging to Christ are the same thing. It explains why Acts 19 treats the twelve as not yet fully Christian until they knew and believed in Jesus. The Spirit is not an extra for the advanced but the mark of every believer.

Pentecost, where tongues first accompanied the Spirit's coming. Acts 19:6 uses the same signs for the same gift, so that Luke can show the work of the Spirit at Ephesus as a continuation of what began in Jerusalem, not a new thing.

The prophet's satire of the idol maker, who burns half a tree for warmth and bows down to the rest. Demetrius and his craftsmen are that satire in the flesh, defending a trade in handmade gods. Paul's line in 19:26 that man-made gods are no gods is Isaiah's argument spoken in a Greek city.

The law's list of practices forbidden to God's people includes divination, sorcery, spells and consulting mediums. The believers of Ephesus who burn their books are obeying a command from Sinai that the pagan city had never heard, and the cost they accept shows how seriously they take it.

Peter's shadow falling on the sick is the earlier twin of Paul's handkerchiefs and aprons. In both places Luke records popular hope and genuine healing without claiming that the shadow or the cloth held power. The healing is credited to God working through His servants.

Paul writes from Ephesus that a great door for effective work has opened to him even though many oppose him. The two halves of that sentence are the two halves of Acts 19, the spreading word and the riot. Opposition and opportunity arrive together.

John's own promise that One more powerful would come, baptizing with the Holy Spirit and with fire. Paul's explanation in 19:4 repeats the point that John pointed beyond himself. The Ephesian twelve are the people still standing in the promise, and their baptism into Jesus brings them into its fulfilment.

God gave Jesus the name above all names so that every knee should bow. The honour given to the name in Acts 19:17 is a small advance of that universal confession. What a city of idol makers and magic scrolls began to see, the whole creation will one day say.

The risen Lord's later letter to Ephesus praises its labour and its rejection of false apostles but warns that it has abandoned its first love. The scrolls and the confessions of Acts 19 show where the church began, and Revelation shows the danger of drifting even from a start that costly.

Paul tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was under a burden beyond his strength and despaired of life, so that he would trust God who raises the dead. It fills in what Luke's triumphant chapter leaves out: the price Paul paid while the word spread.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's opening chapters set humanity under a power that is not merely human. The serpent's voice in Genesis 3 is the first sign, and the story that follows keeps returning to nations that serve what they have made: Babel, Egypt's gods, the Baals of Canaan. Isaiah and the Psalms answer by saying that those gods are empty and that the living God made heaven and earth. Acts 19 is where that argument becomes visible in a first century city. Artemis has a wonder of the world for a house, an economy for a servant and a population for a choir, and the word of the Lord outgrows her without a single act of violence.

The chapter also answers a question that begins in Genesis 12, where God promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham. Here is Asia: Jews and Greeks together hearing the word (19:10), the Spirit given to a new group, and a church planted at the heart of a pagan religion. John the Baptist's preparatory work is gathered in, the Samaritan and Gentile pattern is repeated, and the commission of Acts 1:8 reaches another frontier.

What comes after is already visible in the text. Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome (19:21), and the Ephesian elders will be given their charge at Miletus in the next chapter. The church that begins with scrolls on a bonfire is the church that will receive a letter about the full armour of God, and later a warning from Christ about first love. The story of the churches does not move in a straight line of victories.

The end of the story is Revelation's picture of the nations bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem and of the first things having passed away. In that city there is no temple, no craftsmen of rival gods and no scroll worth burning, because the Lamb is its light. Ephesus is a foretaste: a place where the claim of the Lord Jesus is made on every power, and where, in the end, the only name left standing is His.

quiz.q: Why did Paul question and rebaptize the disciples he met at Ephesus?

options.text: They knew only John's baptism and had not received the Spirit, so he led them to full faith in Jesus.
options.note: They stood between John's preparatory baptism and full faith; Paul completed their understanding, baptized them into Jesus, and the Spirit came.

options.text: Their first baptism was invalid and had to be repeated correctly.
options.note: There is a real deficiency, but the issue was that John's baptism pointed forward and they needed faith in Jesus and His Spirit, not a mere technical repeat.

options.text: They had sinned and needed to be baptized again for forgiveness.
options.note: The issue was not fresh sin but that they were still on the far side of the gospel, knowing only John's baptism.

options.text: It teaches that every believer must be baptized twice.
options.note: This is a unique transitional case, not a rule that all believers be baptized twice.

quiz.q: What happened when the sons of Sceva tried to use the name of Jesus?

options.text: The evil spirit overpowered them, and as a result the name of Jesus was held in high honor.
options.note: They were beaten and fled, and fear and honor for the name of Jesus spread through the city.

options.text: They failed because they did not truly know Jesus.
options.note: True, they lacked real faith, but the fuller point is that their failure led to the name of Jesus being honored and the word prevailing.

options.text: They succeeded at first but later fell away.
options.note: They did not succeed at all; the demon turned on them immediately.

options.text: Nothing happened, since the name of Jesus has no power.
options.note: The opposite: the episode magnified the power of Jesus' name over the demon and the counterfeiters.

quiz.q: What does Luke repeatedly present as the true victor at Ephesus?

options.text: The word of the Lord, which powerfully spread and prevailed.
options.note: Luke's refrain is that the word of the Lord grew and prevailed over magic and idolatry alike.

options.text: The miracles God worked through Paul's hands.
options.note: The miracles were real and striking, but Luke's stated verdict is that the word of the Lord prevailed, not the miracles as such.

options.text: Paul's personal courage in facing the mob.
options.note: Paul was bold, but the disciples kept him from the theatre, and the triumph Luke names is the word of the Lord.

options.text: The town clerk who calmed the riot.
options.note: The clerk restrained the crowd, but he is not presented as the victor; the word of the Lord is.

quiz.q: Why did Demetrius stir up the silversmiths against Paul?

options.text: Paul's preaching that idols are no gods threatened both the cult of Artemis and their income.
options.note: Demetrius names both the loss of trade and the discrediting of Artemis as the danger.

options.text: He was defending the honor of the goddess Artemis.
options.note: He does appeal to Artemis, but Luke shows his first concern was the threat to their prosperity.

options.text: Paul had robbed the temple of Artemis.
options.note: The town clerk explicitly says they had not robbed the temple or blasphemed the goddess.

options.text: The Roman authorities had ordered him to arrest Paul.
options.note: No such order was given; Demetrius stirred up the riot himself over money and the cult.

quiz.q: How did the Ephesian believers show that their faith broke with their past?

options.text: They confessed their deeds and publicly burned their costly magic books.
options.note: Many came forward, confessed, and burned magic books worth fifty thousand drachmas.

options.text: They stopped attending the temple of Artemis.
options.note: Turning from idolatry is implied, but the concrete act Luke records is the confession and burning of magic books.

options.text: They gave away all their money to the poor.
options.note: They destroyed valuable magic books, but the text does not say they gave all their money to the poor.

options.text: They kept their magic quietly in case it was still useful.
options.note: The opposite: they burned the books openly, making a decisive, costly break.

questions: Priscilla and Aquila took Apollos aside and taught him more accurately in private. Who has quietly discipled you, and whom might you help grow without shaming them?
The Ephesian believers burned costly magic books to break with their old life. What would a decisive, even costly, break with your past look like as you follow Christ?
The sons of Sceva tried to use the name of Jesus without knowing Him. Where might you be treating faith as a formula or a technique rather than a real trust in the living Christ?
For two years the word of the Lord spread through patient, daily teaching in a lecture hall. How does that pattern reshape your expectations of how the gospel usually advances?
A whole city rioted to defend a god tied to its wealth and pride. What idols in your own culture, or your own heart, feel threatened when Jesus is truly Lord?

translationNotes.note: The interior renders a phrase that can also be given as the highland, describing Paul's overland route to Ephesus. Footnote markers in the source were omitted when building the verse text.
Fifty thousand drachmas, or pieces of silver, represents an enormous sum, since a drachma was roughly a day's wage; the figure shows the costly, decisive break the new believers made with the occult.
